Section 2.  The appropriation to the Manassas City Public Schools shall be legally
controlled at the total appropriation level. Appropriations to all other operating funds shall
be legally controlled at the fund level. Amendments to the budget and appropriations may
be made in accordance with the City’s Financial Policies (#P-2016-01) and in accordance with
the subsequent sections of this Resolution (#R-2026-971).

Section 3.  The attached budget for the first year (FY 2027) of the Five-Year Capital
Improvement Program is hereby adopted and appropriated in the amount of $76,146,000
for capital projects and $8,743,000 in maintenance capital projects and is legally controlled
at the total appropriation level and will remain in effect until completion of the projects. The
appropriation of these funds is in addition to the appropriations listed in Section 1 of this
Resolution. In order to help fulfill local match requirements needed to be able to utilize City
NVTA 30% revenues, an amount of $300,000 for the City’s Virginia Railway Express
obligation is authorized to be budgeted and appropriated in the NVTA Capital Projects Fund.
The appropriation of these funds is in addition to the appropriations listed in Section 1 of
this Resolution.

Section 4.  All outstanding encumbrances at June 30, 2026, estimated to be $5,000,000
for the City and $1,000,000 for Manassas City Public Schools, are hereby reappropriated to
the FY 2027 budget for the same purpose for which they were appropriated in the previous
fiscal year. The reappropriation of these funds is in addition to the appropriations listed in
Section 1 of this Resolution. All reappropriated funds are monitored and may be lowered
throughout the fiscal year. Upon completion of an encumbrance, staff is authorized to close
out and transfer remaining balances, as needed.

Section 5.  All outstanding grants at June 30, 2026, estimated to be $2,000,000 for the
City and $2,000,000 for Manassas City Public Schools, are hereby reappropriated to the FY
2027 budget for the same purpose for which they were appropriated in the previous fiscal
year. The reappropriation of these funds is in addition to the appropriations listed in Section
1 of this Resolution. All reappropriated funds are monitored and may be lowered
throughout the fiscal year. Upon completion of a grant, staff is authorized to close out and
transfer remaining balances, as needed.

Section 6.  Appropriations for capital projects and maintenance capital projects will
remain in effect until completion of the project, therefore, appropriations unexpended as of
June 30, 2026, estimated to be $160,000,000 for the City and $13,000,000 for Manassas City
Public Schools, are hereby reappropriated to the FY 2027 budget for those projects. The
reappropriation of these funds is in addition to the appropriations listed in Section 1 of this
Resolution. Upon completion of a project, staff is authorized to close out the project and
transfer remaining balances, as needed.

Section 7.  The attached FY 2027 Staffing Plan and Classification and Compensation Plan
are authorized by Council. Modifications may be made in accordance with City of Manassas
Ordinance Relating to Financial Administration of the City (#O-2024-07).

Section 8.  The attached 2026-2030 Strategic Action Plan is hereby approved. All City
departments will annually identify strategies and actions to achieve the goals outlined in this
action plan, and success measures shall be tracked and updated annually as part of the
annual budget process and on the City’s website.

Section 9.  This Resolution shall take effect July 1, 2026.

Michelle Davis-Younger MAYOR
On Behalf of the City Council
of Manassas, Virginia

Introduction

The City of Manassas 2026-2030: Strategic Action Plan is a community based plan for our City’s future. The Plan
provides a framework for action by the City's governing body, administration and community partners over the next
five years of where we would like to be and measures to align our efforts and budgeting for community success. It
articulates a shared vision for our community that is consistent throughout the City's planning documents and is
based on continuous community input and feedback. The plan provides focus for City Departments and ensures
that the City of Manassas elected leadership and government administration are fully in sync. The Plan is divided
into five areas of priorities that identify goals and measures. Our Strategic Action Plan establishes a living roadmap
to ensure Manassas is a vibrant and thriving community in the future.

3 / CITY OF MANASSAS STRATEGIC PLAN
Community Vitality

Why it matters
In the 2024 Community Survey, 79% of responses rated the City as an excellent or good place to live. Overall priorities include the flow
of traffic & ease of getting around the City, the quality of public education, enforcement of City codes & ordinances, and the quality of
economic development. Of the 2024 survey responses 50% have lived in the City more than 20 years, with an additional 16% residing here
for 11-20 years. Additionally, 71% of survey responses plan on living in Manassas in the next 2-5 years.

Goal 1
Increase the supply of diverse housing options while preserving the quality and character of the existing housing stock.

Success measures  1. Increase in the total number of new diverse housing developments to serve residents of
varying income levels.

2. Increase in the total number of first-time homebuyers through local, state, and federal
resources and an increase in housing counseling events through City efforts.

3. Overall satisfaction with the availability of quality housing will increase to greater than 36%.

Goal 2
Ensure that all neighborhoods have access to attractive and safe gathering spaces, parks and trails.

Success measures  1. Increase in the number of lane miles added to the City’s bike and trail network to provide new
connections for modes of travel.

2. Update the Parks, Culture, and Recreation Master Plan to identify, increase, and enhance
neighborhood and community spaces.

3. Increase in the number of identified neighborhood common spaces for the next update of the
parks needs assessment.

4. Continued expansion of programs and offerings at the City of Manassas Community Center.

5. Advance the design of the new Fire Station No 1.

4 / CITY OF MANASSAS STRATEGIC PLAN
Community Vitality

Goal 3
Enhance public safety and preserve community identity.

Success measures  1. The percentage of residents reporting an overall feeling of safety will be maintained at 88% or
greater.

2. Maintain proactive code enforcement and increase education to reduce blight and encourage
well maintained neighborhoods. Code cases will be resolved within 45 business days or
referred to the City Attorney at 95% or greater.

3. Implementation of interdepartmental task force that will increase compliance of City codes &
ordinances within 30 days of violation notice.

Goal 4
Enhance citizen satisfaction with the City as a place to live and strengthen the overall sense of community.

Success measures  1. Overall opinion of the City as a place to live will be maintained at 79% or greater.

2. Increase in community participation and feedback during City hosted events such as, National
Night Out, Community Conversations, the City of Manassas Farmer’s Market, etc.

3. Increase in positive survey results based on studies throughout City departments (i.e., Housing
Survey, Community Feedback Survey, Mobility & Transportation Survey, etc.).

5 / CITY OF MANASSAS STRATEGIC PLAN
Economic Prosperity

Why it matters
A thriving business community is necessary to support local employment opportunities and to generate tax revenue from sources
other than residential real estate. The City is a net importer of jobs with many more people commuting into the City than commuting
out. Quarterly tracking of businesses in the City provide a solid platform in which to base the economic prosperity of Manassas,
with an average of 3.6% of vacant commercial properties since 2021. The City will facilitate development opportunities that support
and enhance the stability of the local economic base and provide residents with a wide array of employment, shopping, and dining
options through a commitment of good governance and planning. The City is committed to support entrepreneurship within our
community so that small businesses can flourish and expand the distinctive character of our Historic Downtown.

Goal 1
Position the City as one of the top communities for businesses in the National Capital Region.

Success measures  1. Overall satisfaction with the City as a place to work will be maintained at 56% or greater.

2. The percentage of residents who are satisfied or very satisfied with the City’s ability to attract
and retain full-time private sector jobs will increase to above 38%.

3. Unemployment in the City will be at or below national and state averages.

4. Consistent and ongoing review of City Codes and development regulations to limit business
development impediments.

Goal 2
Position the City as one of the top communities for residents in the National Capital Region.

Success measures  1. The percentage of residents who are satisfied with the overall quality of life in the City will be
maintained at 67% or greater.

2. Attendance at events and to attractions will increase by 5% annually.

3. There will be an increase in positive press coverage of Manassas and its neighborhoods.

4. Increase in attainable housing options in new development.

Economic Prosperity

Goal 3
Pursue transformative development/redevelopment and leverage assets such as major employers, the Manassas Regional
Airport (HEF), UVA Health Prince William Medical Center and George Mason University.

Success measures  1. Overall satisfaction with efforts to improve existing commercial corridors by redeveloping
blighted or vacant businesses and shopping centers will increase to above 36%.

2. Successful implementation of redevelopment plans for the Mathis Shopping Center and
Downtown opportunity sites, including the former Olde Towne Inn and MIFCO properties.

3. There will be a continued upward trend in private investment in key character areas such as
Godwin Technology/Landings at Cannon Branch and Sudley Medical as well as along business
corridors.

4. Published development timelines will be met 95% of the time.

5. Sales and meals tax receipts will increase by 3% annually respectively.

Goal 4
Continue to partner with Historic Manassas Inc. to advance tourism initiatives within the City.

Success measures  1. Develop outstanding marketing programs to inform the surrounding NOVA community about
City/HMI events.

2. Maintain and enhance the attraction to existing City/HMI events.

3. Identify partnership opportunities to enhance tourism related activities.

7 / CITY OF MANASSAS STRATEGIC PLAN
Advancing Mobility

Why it matters
Manassas’s arterial roads serve as a major transportation component for a majority of Prince William County residents to access both
the City businesses and the rest of Northern Virginia. Based on the 2024 Community Survey, the flow of traffic and ease of getting
around the City ranked as the top priority with 46% answering that this is the most important priority for the City.
Northern Virginia is known for its long commutes to work, with a mean commute time of 26.6 minutes according to the 2023 U.S.
American Community Survey. In Manassas, that commute time is 33 minutes and 69% of our commuters drive alone to work. Based
on the 2024 Community Survey, the flow of traffic and ease of getting around the City ranked as the top priority with 46% answering
that this is the most important priority for the City. Options to construct new roads within the City are extremely limited so growing
alternative modes of travel and enhancing transit options will become increasingly important as the City continues to grow.

Goal 1
Increase community satisfaction with ease of traveling within the City by improving the City’s transportation network,
resulting in a safer, more secure, more reliable, and more convenient system for all to use.

Success measures  1. Reduction in the number of collisions City-wide and at the top five accident locations
identified.

2. Increase in the number of traffic calming projects.

3. Increase in the City’s Walk Score and recognition as a Walkable City instead of a Car-Depen-
dent City.

4. Increase in the percentage of residents that are very satisfied with the ease of access to
information about City projects and the City’s efforts to keep residents informed about local
issues.

5. Develop and adopt strategies that keep our community safely in motion.

Goal 2
Increase the percentage of mode share of alternatives to driving alone, resulting in a more convenient, more affordable, and
less congested transportation system for all residents to use.

Success measures  1. Increase in the ratio of the total bicycle network mileage to total road network mileage.

2. Decrease in the number of residents commuting by single occupancy vehicle to below 69%.

3. Increase in the amount of available parking in the downtown and in neighborhoods.

4. Decrease in percentage of households with three or more vehicles to below 26%.

5. Progress towards achieving Silver Level Bicycle Friendly Community recognition within five
years.

Advancing Mobility

Goal 3
Develop collaborations with all relevant transportation stakeholders to leverage existing and emerging technologies and infra-
structure to optimize its transportation system.

Success measures  1. Increase in transit ridership generally and growth in VRE reverse ridership.

2. Identify location for a City Mobility Hub that will increase the number of modes and amenities
offered at a central location.

3. Increase in the number of corridors that are ADA accessible.

Goal 4
Align the City’s transportation system with land use objectives in a way that supports sustained economic vitality.

Success measures  1. Increase in the number of residents that both live and work in the city.

2. Reach the 2030 Targets identified in the Mobility Master Plan (2026-2030).

3. Implementation of the City’s CIP Transportation projects.

Educational Success

Why it matters
An individual’s level of education and skill training has a direct impact on income, skills and the opportunities that people have to lead
healthier lives in their community, and its importance cannot be overstated. In 2023 Manassas, 82% of the City’s population has a high
school degree or higher compared to 90% in Prince William County and 91% in Virginia. Accordingly, Manassas residents ranked the
quality of education as one of their top priorities in the 2024 Citizen Satisfaction Survey with 40% responding it is the most important,
and 37% of responses were satisfied with the quality of public education, and that and only 52% of residents rate the City satisfactory
as a Place to Raise & Educate Children, compared to 61% of residents across the U.S. that were asked the same question about their
communities.

Goal 1
Develop multiple pathways to success allowing all students (public, private, and home school) to reach their full potential.

Success measures  1. The percentage of Manassas students graduating from high school by 2030 will equal or
exceed the state average.

2. The percentage of working adults in Manassas with milestone credentials (i.e. a High School
Diploma/GED, Associates Degree/Certification or Bachelor’s Degree) will meet or exceed
regional averages.

3. Add at least two unique partnerships between educational institutions and City government
or businesses.

4. Maximize allocated seats of Manassas preschoolers enrolled in an early childhood initiative.

Ensure that the education system within the City is welcoming and open, communicates successes and opportunities with
students and parents, and builds new relationships within the community.

Success measures  1. The percentage of residents that rate the City satisfactory as a place to raise and educate
children will increase to above 52%.
